questions.stem: A 19-year-old man presented with rectal prolapse. He had arrived in the UK 2 weeks earlier. He was normally resident in Vietnam. He reported recurrent intermittent episodes of mild abdominal pain for as long as he can remember. On examination he appeared small in stature, but otherwise the exam was unremarkable. Feces microscopy for ova, cysts and parasites:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely infective cause?
questions.explanation: Trichuris trichiura The most likely organism here is Trichuris trichiura. Rectal prolapse is a known complication of this infection. Trichuris ova are typically 50 × 20 μm in size and are barrel-shaped. They have a smooth wall with a hyaline plug at both ends. Egg numbers usually correlate with adult worm burden. (Image from Bogitsh B, Carter C, Oeltman T , eds. Human Parasitology. 5th ed. Elsevier; 2019.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q33

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man presented with acute breathlessness, wheeze, and severe abdominal pain. He had a past medical history of allergic rhinitis which he controlled with antihistamines as required. One week earlier he had been diagnosed with temporal arteritis for which he started a course of high-dose oral prednisolone. He denied excessive alcohol use, smoking, or consuming any illicit drug use. He lived in Peru until age 18 years when he emigrated to the UK for work. On examination the patient was unwell. Vitals revealed respiratory rate 28 breaths/minute, oxygen saturations 92% on 15 L/minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, heart rate 124 beats/minute, and temperature 38.5°C. He had a diffuse wheeze throughout his chest and was unable to complete sentences. He had generalized abdominal pain with no guarding and normal bowel sounds. Initial investigations: Hemoglobin: 132 g/L (135–180) Total WCC: 20.8 ×109/L (4.0–11.0) (neutrophils 15.2, lymphocytes 1.5, monocytes 1.1) Platelets: 178 ×109/L (150–450) Urea: 9.2 mmol/L (2.8–8.1) Creatinine: 112 μmol/L (62–106) Amylase: 1250 U/L (60–180) Cholesterol and triglycerides were normal Urgent chest X-ray: Urgent abdominal USS revealed sludge in a normal gallbladder but no gallstones or blockage of common bile or cystic duct.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfestation Strongyloides hyperinfestation is the most likely condition. Strongyloides are nematodes (roundworms) that may be acquired from dogs and other companion animals, but also from soil or other materials contaminated with human feces. Countries in South America (particularly Peru) have a high prevalence of Strongyloides infection, and consequently latent asymptomatic infection is common. Hyperinfestation illness can occur in patients with underlying asymptomatic disease who become immunosuppressed, as in this case with high-dose steroids. Consider asking patients about clinical manifestations of initial infection (rash, respiratory symptoms). Strongyloides-associated pancreatitis is a recognized feature of hyperinfestation illness but remains an infrequent cause of acute pancreatitis, particularly in immunocompetent hosts. The patient’s total leucocyte count and neutrophil count is raised. Neutrophilia commonly reflects bacterial infection, but it should be noted that steroids cause an accelerated release of neutrophils from the bone marrow. As a result neutrophilia is commonly seen in patients receiving steroid therapy. In this scenario the total leucocyte count is not completely accounted for by neutrophils, lymphocytes, or monocytes. This suggests that another leucocyte is raised, such as eosinophils, which would fit with tissue-migratory helminth infection. Acute cholangitis is a common condition although the patient does not have classic risk factors, clinical features, or radiologic findings. Of note, the absence of gallstones or inflammation on USS does not entirely rule this out but does make this condition less likely. The chest X-ray reveals bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, which are seen in SIRS, but can also be seen in other conditions including atypical pneumonia and hyperinfestation illness. Community-acquired pneumonia caused by mycoplasma can present as severe shortness of breath with extrapulmonary features such as pancreatitis. Despite this, the clinical situation is atypical for mycoplasma infection as it is most common in patients <40 years old, symptoms crescendo over 2–3weeks, and are commonly associated with cough and headaches (absent in the patient). Blood tests can also reveal a hemolytic anemia (again absent). Adult-onset asthma is plausible, particularly as he has a history of atopy, but this is uncommon, and the association of other features (pancreatitis) makes this unlikely. Acute HIV classically presents as an infectious mononucleosis-type illness with fever, rash, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy. Atypical presentations with involvement of different body systems can occur but as the patient does not have clear risk factors (although these should be clarified) and lymphocyte count is normal, this would make acute HIV unlikely. An HIV test should still be performed. (Image from Wang Y, Ma Y, Xu Y, et al. Strongyloides stercoralis disseminated infection in a patient misdiagnosed with chronic asthmatic bronchitis. J Microbiol Immunol Infect. 2016;49(1):154–156.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q17

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man was reviewed with longstanding generalized abdominal pain. He had moved to the UK 4 years previously from Uganda where he had been born and brought up. Clinical examination was unremarkable. Investigations: Hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL MCV 69 fL Eosinophil count 0.5 ×109/L Feces microscopy for ova, cysts, and parasites ×1: negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Albendazole The history of chronic abdominal pain, microcytic anemia, mild eosinophilia, and epidemiologic exposure is most likely to be explained by a hookworm infection. Albendazole (or mebendazole) is used most frequently as first-line treatment. Iron replacements may be used, but anemia will recur without specific treatment to clear the parasites. Pyrantel is a good alternative; ivermectin has poor activity against hookworm. There is no indication for DEC.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q32

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man was reviewed for ongoing epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He had been born and brought up in Thailand and had moved to the United States age 18. Investigation: Peripheral eosinophil count 1.4 ×109/L Stool OCP ×3 negative Strongyloides serology positive
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ivermectin While both ivermectin and albendazole have activity against Strongyloides, ivermectin has a better reported efficacy. Pentamidine, praziquantel, and suramin have no role in the treatment of strongyloidiasis.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of nausea, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. She had received a deceased donor kidney transplant for polycystic kidney disease 3 months prior. She had received antithymocyte globulin for induction and was on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone for maintenance immunosuppression. She rapidly developed a purpuric rash and respiratory failure and required intubation. Gross hematuria was seen on urinary catheterization. Bronchoscopy: diffuse hemorrhage seen. She was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics.
questions.lead_in: In addition to supportive critical care, what is the best therapeutic intervention?
questions.explanation: Ivermectin per NG The patient has Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome. Light microscopy of urine showed larvae consistent with Strongyloides.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of an itchy rash on her leg. She had returned 2 weeks earlier from a holiday in the Caribbean. On exam:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous larva migrans The rash is characteristic and diagnostic of cutaneous larva migrans (CLM), pruritic, serpiginous, located in lower extremities. CLM is a result of infection by animal hookworm larvae, most commonly Ancylostoma braziliense or A. caninum. These are found worldwide, but infection is commoner in tropical and subtropical regions. The larvae can penetrate the skin but cannot pass through the basement membrane of the epidermis. They migrate slowly at a few centimeters/day, causing an inflammatory response along their track. This manifests as an intensely pruritic, red, raised, serpiginous lesion, usually on a lower extremity, or any part of the body exposed to contaminated sand. The actual larvae are a centimeter or two ahead of the lesion. Lesions normally resolve within 2–8 weeks. Gnathostomiasis can cause localized lesions, but these are associated with edema and pain as well as itching and erythema. Most cases are reported from Asia (especially Thailand and Japan) as well as Mexico. Larva currens is caused by infection with Strongyloides stercoralis. It is also a serpiginous eruption, but the tracks are less defined. They are much faster moving than CLM lesions, at approximately 5 cm/hour, but only last a few hours. Phytophotodermatitis is caused by topical exposure to certain plant substances; commonly lime juice. Irregular itchy blisters and erythematous patches develop on sunexposed skin. Linear lesions are common. Lesions appear 24 hours after sun exposure, are not pruritic, but may be painful. (Image from Kincaid L, Klowak M, Klowak S, Boggild AK. Management of imported cutaneous larva migrans: a case series and mini-review. Travel Med Infect Dis. 2015;13(5):382–387.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q47

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy was reviewed with a 4-week history of mild abdominal discomfort, anorexia, and some loose stools. He was normally resident in California but had returned from 2 months living with family in Mexico 1 month prior to symptom onset. Examination was unremarkable. Investigations: Stool OCP:
questions.lead_in: What parasite is most likely to be causing his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Ascaris lumbricoides The egg seen is that of Ascaris lumbricoides. Stool OCP (ova, cysts, and parasites) microscopy is usually positive in Ascaris infection due to the huge numbers of eggs that are produced and shed. Fertilized eggs are rounded with a thick bumpy outer shell, often stained brown. Abdominal symptoms are often absent or nonspecific unless an adult worm is passed in the stool. It takes around 6–8 weeks after egg ingestion for abdominal symptoms to develop. (Image from Maguire JH. Intestinal nematodes (roundworms). In Bennett JE, Dolin R, Blaser MJ, eds. Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett’s Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases. Updated 8th ed. Elsevier; 2015.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q29

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl was reviewed with nausea and epigastric pain made worse on eating. There was no diarrhea. She had no other medical problems and did not take any regular medications. She was normally resident in Florida but had recently returned from a 3-month stay in Costa Rica with family. Examination was unremarkable. Investigations: Absolute eosinophil count 0.6 ×109/L Stool microscopy:
questions.lead_in: What parasite is most likely to be causing her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Necator americanus This is a hookworm egg. It is not possible to distinguish between Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus on microscopy (that requires the larval stage), but geographically this is more likely to be Necator americanus. (Image from Maguire JH. Intestinal nematodes (roundworms). In Bennett JE, Dolin R, Blaser MJ, eds. Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett’s Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases. Updated 8th ed. Elsevier; 2015.)

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman from Jamaica has a history of chronic, watery diarrhea. Recently, she had to receive highdose steroids for a new diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus. She presents now with several days of fever and headache, and her blood cultures and CSF cultures are growing Escherichia coli.
questions.lead_in: In addition to antibacterial therapy, what additional medications could be considered to treat her underlying condition?
questions.explanation: Ivermectin This patient likely has infection with Strongyloides stercoralis, which is more common in tropical countries. It typically causes infection limited to the lung and GI tract, but, in immunocompromised hosts, it can also cause hyperinfection syndrome that can present as gram-negative bacteremia and meningitis because of parasite-driven translocation of enteric bacteria. Treatment of choice for strongyloidiasis is ivermectin.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q40

parts_raw.text: Do you treat and if yes, what drug: Blastocystis hominis / E. hartmanni / Trichuris trichiura / Strongyloides stercoralis
Sibling travelled, had abdo pain and stool O+P shows E. histolytica/dispar. What one test do you suggest and why?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Blastocystis hominis - generally no; treat only if truly symptomatic with no other cause (metronidazole or TMP-SMX). (2) Entamoeba hartmanni - no; non-pathogenic commensal. (3) Trichuris trichiura - yes; albendazole 400 mg or mebendazole x 3-7 days. (4) Strongyloides stercoralis - yes, always treat even if asymptomatic (autoinfection causes lifelong infection and risk of fatal hyperinfection with future immunosuppression); ivermectin 200 ug/kg daily x 2 days. b) Send a stool Entamoeba histolytica-specific antigen test (Gal/GalNAc lectin) or PCR, because microscopy cannot distinguish pathogenic E. histolytica from non-pathogenic E. dispar/E. moshkovskii.
questions.beyond_mandell: Blastocystis, E. hartmanni and E. histolytica/dispar are protozoa outside this chapter; management per IDSA/Mandell protozoa guidance. Strongyloides always-treat rationale and Trichuris therapy grounded in the chapter (pp. 3441, 3437).

b) What are 2 public health concerns they raise in endemic settings
c) Name two public health strategies for controlling them.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Ascaris lumbricoides. (2) Trichuris trichiura. (3) Hookworm (Necator americanus / Ancylostoma duodenale). b) (1) Iron-deficiency anemia (leading global cause, especially from hookworm; worsens pregnancy outcomes). (2) Impaired child growth/nutrition and cognitive development (growth stunting, vitamin A deficiency, reduced school performance). c) (1) Mass preventive (anthelmintic) chemotherapy / deworming programs targeting at-risk groups. (2) Improved water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) with proper disposal of human/animal feces and access to potable water (plus health education). d) Loeffler syndrome (eosinophilic pneumonitis from larval pulmonary migration); Strongyloides hyperinfection is the other classic non-endemic presentation.

cohort_answer.text: a) Hookworm (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale); Ascaris lumbricoides; Trichuris trichiura. b) Anemia; Vitamin/nutrient deficiency in children; Secondary neurologic complications from nutritional deficiency; Dehydration. c) Treatment of potential hosts (dogs, cats); Mass anthelmintic treatment; Sanitation/Sewage control; Shoes; education. d) Loeffler's syndrome; Strongyloides Hyperinfection.

questions.model_answer: a) In heavy Loa loa co-infection, ivermectin can precipitate a fatal encephalopathy from rapid killing of high-level microfilaremia (a Mazzotti-type reaction); check for Loa loa (blood smear/serology) and consider albendazole pre-treatment before giving ivermectin. b) (1) Screen before immunosuppression with Strongyloides serology (recombinant NIE/SsIR ELISA, near 100% sensitivity) plus stool exams, and treat any positive with ivermectin. (2) If screening is unavailable or high pre-test probability, treat empirically/presumptively with ivermectin, because immunosuppression (especially corticosteroids) can trigger fatal hyperinfection/dissemination in a chronically, lifelong-infected host.

questions.model_answer:
a) Ascaris lumbricoides.
b) Life cycle: Adult worms live in the small intestine; a female releases >200,000 eggs/day passed in feces. Eggs embryonate and become infective in soil over ~2-3 weeks (durable, viable up to years). After a human ingests embryonated eggs (fecal-oral), stage-2 larvae hatch in the small intestine, penetrate the intestinal wall, and travel via the portal circulation to the liver, then via the blood to the lungs. In the lungs larvae molt (L2->L3), migrate up the bronchotracheal tree across the epiglottis, and are swallowed back into the small intestine, where they mature into adults. Egg production is detectable in stool ~2-3 months after ingestion; adult worms live 12-24 months.

cohort_answer.text: Ascaris lumbricoides. Life cycle: adult worms live in lumen of small intestine; female produces ~200,000 eggs/day passed with feces; unfertilized eggs not infective; larvae develop to infectivity within fertile eggs after 18 days to several weeks depending on environment (optimum moist, warm, shaded soil); after infective eggs swallowed, larvae hatch, invade intestinal mucosa, carried via portal then systemic circulation to lungs; mature in lungs (10-14 days), penetrate alveolar walls, ascend bronchial tree to throat, swallowed; develop into adult worms in small intestine; 2-3 months from ingestion of infective eggs to oviposition; adult worms live 1-2 years. (Autoinfection examples: Strongyloides, Paracapillaria, Hymenolepis.)

parts_raw.text: A) Stool O+P is done - indicate which of the following should be treated and with what? Organism | Treatment: Strongyloides stercoralis; Trichuris trichiura; Dientamoeba fragilis; Entamoeba hartmanii
B) Husband found to have entamoeba histolytica/dispar in stool. What is one step you would do next, how would it help you?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Strongyloides stercoralis – YES, treat: ivermectin 200 µg/kg daily × 2 days (cures ~93%); always treat given lifelong autoinfection and hyperinfection risk. (2) Trichuris trichiura – YES, treat: albendazole 400 mg PO × 3–7 days or mebendazole 500 mg daily (or 100 mg BID) × 3–7 days (single-dose therapy has poor cure rates for whipworm). (3) Dientamoeba fragilis – no treatment required in an asymptomatic patient whose diarrhea has resolved. (4) Entamoeba hartmanni – NO, a non-pathogenic ameba, do not treat.
b) Perform a specific test to distinguish E. histolytica from the morphologically identical non-pathogenic E. dispar – a stool antigen (EIA) test or PCR; only E. histolytica is pathogenic and warrants treatment, so this determines whether the husband needs therapy.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ivermectin dosing/cure rate and Trichuris regimens are from this chapter; Dientamoeba fragilis and Entamoeba (hartmanni, histolytica/dispar) are protozoa not covered here – pathogenicity and E. histolytica/dispar differentiation by antigen EIA/PCR are from IDSA/CDC amebiasis guidance. Pre-ivermectin Loa loa screening (endemic in Cameroon) is also outside this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides stercoralis - Yes: Ivermectin 200 ug/kg for 2 days or 1 dose repeated 2 weeks after (screen for hypermicrofilaremia with loa loa prior to treatment); Trichuris trichiura - Yes: Mebendazole 500mg PO daily x3 days (superior to albendazole); Dientamoeba fragilis - No; Entamoeba hartmanii - No (non-pathogenic amebae). B) E. histolytica confirmed by trophozoites containing ingested erythrocytes or positive immunoassay AND PCR; PCR differentiates histolytica from dispar - gold standard, 100x more sensitive than antigen assay, up to 100% specific; facilitates early diagnosis and can follow treatment response.

questions.question: A patient has Strongyloides with filarial co-infection.
questions.question_raw: Q79 (2012 AM). Strongyloides with filarial co-infection.

parts.text: What is the risk of ivermectin?
Give two ways to manage a person from a Strongyloides-endemic region who is about to start immunosuppression.

parts_raw.text: A) What is the risk of ivermectin?
B) 2 ways to handle those from an endemic region for strongyloides going to start immunosuppression?

questions.model_answer:
a) In a patient co-infected with Loa loa who has high-level microfilaremia, ivermectin can precipitate a severe, potentially fatal encephalopathy; therefore screen for Loa loa before giving ivermectin in Loa-endemic areas and use albendazole as an alternative if heavy loiasis is confirmed.
b) (1) Screen ("test") – serology for Strongyloides (and stool studies) and treat those who are positive with ivermectin before starting immunosuppression. (2) Empiric ("presumptive") treatment – give ivermectin to at-risk patients before, or without waiting for, test results, given the high mortality of steroid-induced hyperinfection.
questions.beyond_mandell: The ivermectin–Loa loa encephalopathy risk is from filariasis/loiasis literature (Mandell filariasis chapter, WHO), not this intestinal-nematode chapter, which only establishes that steroids/immunosuppression precipitate Strongyloides hyperinfection. The screen-and-treat vs empiric-treat strategies are standard pre-immunosuppression Strongyloides practice.

cohort_answer.text: A) Administration of ivermectin to highly loa loa microfilaremic subjects can precipitate life-threatening encephalopathy. Relative contraindications: confirmed/suspected loa loa infection (albendazole alternative), previous hypersensitivity, weight<15kg or age<1 year, pregnant women (category C). B) 'Test and treat' approach; empiric administration of ivermectin to at-risk patients before immunosuppression before results are back.

questions.question: A recent immigrant has eosinophilia but a negative stool ova and parasites, with no real symptoms. Serology is positive for Strongyloides and Schistosoma; stool ova and parasites is negative.
questions.question_raw: Q29 (2010 PM). Patient recently immigrated who has eosinophilia, but stool O+P negative. No real symptoms otherwise. Positive serology for Strongyloides and Schistosomiasis. Stool O+P negative

parts.text: Give the three most common causes of asymptomatic eosinophilia in this patient.
Give two reasons the stool ova and parasites is negative.

parts_raw.text: A) Give 3 most common causes for asymptomatic eosinophilia in this patient
B) Give 2 reasons why the stool O+P is negative

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Strongyloides stercoralis. (2) Schistosoma species. (3) Hookworm (Necator americanus/Ancylostoma spp.). These soil-transmitted/tissue helminths are the most commonly identified parasites causing incidental eosinophilia in returning travellers/immigrants.
b) (1) Intermittent/low-level larval or egg excretion with low sensitivity of stool microscopy – Strongyloides sheds larvae intermittently, so up to ~7 stool examinations are needed to detect it. (2) It can take several weeks after infection for larvae/eggs to appear in stool (pre-patent period), and Schistosoma (S. haematobium) eggs may not be passed in stool at all; serology detects infection before/without stool positivity.
questions.beyond_mandell: Schistosoma is not covered in this chapter; its role as a common cause of eosinophilia and its stool-insensitivity (S. haematobium eggs in urine) are from the schistosomiasis chapter/CDC. The chapter supports Strongyloides and hookworm and the poor sensitivity/intermittent excretion of stool testing.

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides, Schistosomiasis, and hookworm are most commonly identified parasites (network +REDIVI data: S. stercoralis 34.4%, Schistosoma sp 11.0%, hookworm 8.6%). Other infectious causes: Filariae, HIV-1, various helminths. Non-infectious: allergy/atopic disease, drug reaction, hypoadrenalism, tumor-associated, hypereosinophilic syndromes. B) Stool O+P is very insensitive for Strongyloides (intermittent shedding) and Schistosomiasis; parasite not always excreted in stool (S. haematobium eggs excreted in urine not stool); for strongyloides eggs degrade before leaving body, need to look for rhabditiform larvae specifically; interval from acquisition to positive test result can be 3-4 weeks before GI symptoms/worms in intestine.

questions.question: Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome.

parts.text: Define/explain Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome.
Give two treatments.

parts_raw.text: A) Define/explain strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome
Give 2 treatments

questions.model_answer:
a) Hyperinfection syndrome is accelerated autoinfection in an immunosuppressed host: larvae penetrating the gut and adult worms in the gastrointestinal tract accumulate in massively increased numbers within the normal autoinfection cycle. It is most often precipitated by corticosteroids (or underlying HTLV-1 infection), can occur within days of steroid therapy, and larvae invading the gut mucosa carry enteric bacteria into the blood, causing gram-negative/polymicrobial bacteremia, meningitis, septic shock, and pneumonitis; untreated mortality is 35–100%. (Dissemination = worms found at ectopic extra-intestinal sites; both are diagnosed by finding larvae in body fluids outside the GI tract.)
b) (1) High-dose ivermectin 200 µg/kg daily for at least 14 days (oral). (2) In patients unable to take oral medication, parenteral/rectal/subcutaneous ivermectin (a veterinary formulation used under compassionate-use protocol).
questions.beyond_mandell: The commonly quoted adjunctive albendazole 400 mg BID with ivermectin for hyperinfection is not specified in this chapter (chapter lists ivermectin as the cornerstone, 14+ days for disseminated disease, with alternative routes when oral is not possible).

cohort_answer.text: Hyperinfection syndrome occurs when low cellular immunity leads to strongyloides dissemination with extra-intestinal involvement, typically due to steroids or concurrent HTLV infection; accelerated autoinfection with higher parasite quantity in typical autoinfection cycle locations; often associated with gram negative sepsis. Disseminated strongyloidiasis = hyperinfection with spread to organs/tissues outside autoinfection cycle (skin, lungs, GI); both diagnosed by finding parasite in fluid outside GI tract. Treatment: Ivermectin 200ug/kg/d x2 weeks minimum PLUS Albendazole 400mg PO BID x7 days.

questions.question: A woman who immigrated from India 6 years ago now has asymptomatic eosinophilia documented on 3 occasions over the past 3 months, with an elevated IgE. LFTs are normal, occult blood is negative, and stool ova and parasites are negative.

parts.text: Name the top 3 diagnoses.
List 3 investigations you would do next.

parts_raw.text: A) Name the top 3 diagnoses
B) List 3 investigations you would do next

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Strongyloides stercoralis (chronic autoinfection, can persist for decades after emigration; stool O+P frequently negative). (2) Lymphatic filariasis / occult filarial infection (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia spp.) given endemic India origin. (3) Schistosomiasis (chronic tissue helminth causing persistent eosinophilia). b) (1) Strongyloides serology (IgG ELISA) - more sensitive than stool. (2) Filarial studies: nocturnal (10pm-2am) blood smear for microfilariae plus filarial serology (antifilarial IgG4) or circulating antigen. (3) Schistosoma serology, and HIV serology as a contributor/coinfection to screen.

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides stercoralis; Schistosomiasis; HIV; Helminths (filariasis). B) HIV serology; Strongyloides serology; Schistosoma serology; Stool ova + parasite; Filarial serology.

questions.question: Geohelminths (soil-transmitted helminths).
questions.question_raw: Q77 (2012 AM, 2011 PM, 2009 AM). Geohelminths

parts.text: Give the definition.
Apart from Strongyloides, name three others.
What two public health concerns do they cause in endemic areas?
Give two public health strategies for control.
What syndromes do they cause in developed countries/non-endemic regions?

parts_raw.text: A) Definition:
B) Apart from Strongyloides, name 3 others
C) What 2 public health concerns do they cause in endemic areas?
D) 2 public health strategies for control
E) Syndromes in developed countries/non-endemic regions

questions.model_answer:
a) Soil-transmitted helminths: intestinal nematodes whose life cycle requires a phase of maturation in soil, with human infection by fecal-oral ingestion of embryonated eggs or dermal penetration of soil-dwelling larvae.
b) (1) Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm). (2) Trichuris trichiura (whipworm). (3) Hookworm (Necator americanus/Ancylostoma duodenale).
c) (1) Iron-deficiency anemia (especially hookworm) and malnutrition/vitamin A deficiency. (2) Growth stunting and impaired cognitive development in children (with reduced school participation and economic productivity).
d) (1) Mass preventive chemotherapy (mass drug administration with albendazole/mebendazole to high-risk groups). (2) Improvements in water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) – proper disposal of feces, potable water, and health education (e.g., wearing shoes).
e) In non-endemic/developed settings they present as: incidental asymptomatic eosinophilia; Loeffler syndrome/pneumonitis during larval lung migration (Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides – not Trichuris, which has no lung phase); Strongyloides hyperinfection/dissemination in the immunosuppressed; Ascaris intestinal (small-bowel) obstruction or biliary disease; and Trichuris colitis/rectal prolapse.

cohort_answer.text: A) Soil transmitted helminths - part of life cycle involves living in soil. B) Ascaris lumbricoides; Trichuris trichiura (whipworm); Necator americanus (hookworm); Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm). C) Anemia; Malnutrition; Stunting/poor growth/failure to thrive; Developmental delay. D) Mass drug administration; Improving sanitation; Public education (e.g. wearing shoes). E) Asymptomatic eosinophilia; Loeffler's syndrome (except Trichuris, no lung phase); Strongyloides hyperinfection; Trichuris prolapsed rectum; Ascaris bowel obstruction.

questions.question: Among the soil-transmitted helminths, which one is acquired by oral ingestion yet has a tissue (lung) migratory phase?

parts.text: Which soil-transmitted helminth is acquired by oral ingestion but has a tissue migratory phase?
Draw the life cycle for this organism.

parts_raw.text: Of the soil-transmitted helminths, which one has oral ingestion but tissue migratory phase?
Draw the life cycle for this one

questions.model_answer:
a) Ascaris lumbricoides.
b) Life cycle: (1) Embryonated eggs are ingested (fecal-oral) from contaminated soil/food. (2) Stage-2 larvae hatch in the small intestine and penetrate the intestinal wall. (3) They are carried by the portal vasculature to the liver, then via the blood to the lungs. (4) In the lung parenchyma larvae molt (L2→L3), migrate up the bronchotracheal tree across the epiglottis, and are swallowed. (5) Back in the small intestine they mature into adult worms (living 1–2 years); females release >200,000 eggs/day, which are passed in stool and embryonate in soil, completing the cycle.

cohort_answer.text: Ascaris lumbricoides.

questions.question: Give the treatment for each of these parasites: pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis); Hymenolepis nana; and a third parasite (not recalled).
questions.question_raw: Q81 (2008). Treatment for these 3 parasites: Pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis); Hymenolepsis nana; [third parasite not recalled by author]

parts.text: Give the treatment for each parasite.

parts_raw.text: Give treatment for each parasite

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm): pyrantel pamoate 11 mg/kg once (max 1 g) or albendazole 400 mg once, repeated in 2 weeks; treat all household contacts and wash bedding/clothing. (2) Hymenolepis nana: praziquantel (single dose) – a cestode, not covered in this chapter. (3) Third parasite: not recalled/unknown.
questions.beyond_mandell: Hymenolepis nana is a cestode (praziquantel) not covered by this intestinal-nematode chapter; treatment is from the cestode chapter/CDC.

cohort_answer.text: Pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis) - mebendazole. Hymenolepsis nana - praziquantel (cestode causing weakness, headaches, anorexia, abdominal pain, diarrhea). Third parasite: not recalled.

questions.question: List three nematodes with a lung phase.

parts.text: List three nematodes with a lung (migratory) phase.

parts_raw.text: List 3 nematodes with a lung phase

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Ascaris lumbricoides. (2) Strongyloides stercoralis. (3) Hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale/Necator americanus). All three migrate from gut or skin through the venous system to the lungs, up the trachea, and are swallowed (see Fig. 286.1).

cohort_answer.text: Ascaris lumbricoides; Strongyloides stercoralis; Hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus); Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi (tropical pulmonary eosinophilia). (Note: Paragonimiasis is NOT a nematode, it is a trematode.) Essentially any cause of Loeffler's syndrome has a lung phase.

The patient's husband has Entamoeba histolytica/dispar in stool – what test differentiates the Entamoeba?
questions.question_raw: Choice of agent and whether to treat or not for: Strongyloides; Trichuris trichiura; Entamoeba hartmanii; Blastocystis (no symptoms). A patient's husband has Entamoeba histolytica/dispar in the stool. What test to differentiate the Entamoeba?

parts.text: Strongyloides – treat, and with what?
Trichuris trichiura – treat, and with what?
Entamoeba hartmanni – treat?
Blastocystis (no symptoms) – treat?
What test differentiates E. histolytica from E. dispar?

parts_raw.text: Strongyloides - treat and with what?
Trichuris trichiura - treat and with what?
Entamoeba hartmanii - treat?
Blastocystis (no symptoms) - treat?
Test to differentiate E. histolytica/dispar

questions.model_answer:
a) Strongyloides: YES – ivermectin 200 µg/kg daily × 2 days (14+ days if disseminated).
b) Trichuris trichiura: YES – albendazole 400 mg × 3–7 days or mebendazole 500 mg daily (or 100 mg BID) × 3–7 days; single-dose therapy has poor cure rates.
c) Entamoeba hartmanni: NO – non-pathogenic ameba.
d) Blastocystis (asymptomatic): NO – do not treat.
e) A stool antigen enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or PCR that specifically detects E. histolytica – microscopy cannot distinguish the pathogenic E. histolytica from the identical non-pathogenic E. dispar; only E. histolytica requires treatment (luminal agent ± tissue amebicide).
questions.beyond_mandell: Entamoeba (hartmanni, histolytica/dispar) and Blastocystis are protozoa not covered in this chapter; their (non-)pathogenicity and the histolytica/dispar antigen-EIA/PCR differentiation are from IDSA/CDC amebiasis guidance. Strongyloides and Trichuris regimens are grounded in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Strongyloides: Yes - Ivermectin 1-2 days (non-disseminated). Trichuris trichiura: Yes - Mebendazole x3 days (100mg orally BID x3 days, adults and children). Entamoeba hartmanii: No. Blastocystis (asymptomatic): No. Test: EIA allows E. histolytica differentiation. Treatment if E. histolytica confirmed: asymptomatic = intraluminal agent only (paromomycin x7d); diarrhea/extraintestinal = flagyl 750mg PO TID x7d then intraluminal agent (paromomycin x7d).
